summary: Following the first revelation, the Prophet ﷺ called people to Islam quietly and privately for approximately three years, beginning with his closest family and friends. This period saw the formation of the first nucleus of the Muslim community, as individuals from various backgrounds accepted the message one by one.
narrative:
After the first revelation in the Cave of Hira and the commencement of prophethood, Allah did not immediately instruct the Prophet ﷺ to call all of Makkah openly. The early period, spanning approximately 610 to 613 CE, was characterized by quiet, personal invitation — each new Muslim brought in through direct relationship, persuasion, and the evident truth of the message.

The first to accept Islam was Khadijah bint Khuwaylid (RA), the Prophet's wife, who affirmed her belief on the very night of the first revelation without a moment's hesitation. Her immediate and unwavering acceptance is recorded by every major biographer including Ibn Hisham, Ibn Sa'd, and al-Tabari. She was followed by Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA) — who was then a young boy living in the Prophet's household — and by Zayd ibn Harithah (RA), the freed slave who was like a son to the Prophet ﷺ.

Among adults outside the household, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) was the first free adult male to accept Islam. Ibn Kathir records in al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah that when the Prophet ﷺ presented Islam to him, Abu Bakr accepted immediately without hesitation — a distinction the Prophet ﷺ himself later acknowledged. Abu Bakr then set about calling his own network of trusted friends, bringing to Islam within the early period: Uthman ibn Affan, Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sad ibn Abi Waqqas, and Talhah ibn Ubaydallah — men who would later become among the most eminent of the Companions.

Others who accepted Islam in this early phase include Khadijah's cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal (though he died shortly after the first revelation), Bilal ibn Rabah (RA) who was enslaved by the Banu Jumah, Ammar ibn Yasir (RA) and his parents Yasir and Sumayyah — who would become the first martyrs of Islam — and Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam (RA), in whose house the Prophet ﷺ would later gather the early Muslims.

The house of al-Arqam on the hill of al-Safa in Makkah became the primary gathering place for this nascent community. Ibn Hisham notes that the Prophet ﷺ would meet his followers there, teach them the Quran as it was revealed, instruct them in prayer, and strengthen their faith and brotherhood. This house served as something between a safehouse and a school during the years when open preaching was not yet commanded.

During this period, the early Muslims prayed quietly, often in the valleys outside Makkah where they would not be seen by hostile Quraysh. Ibn Sa'd records an incident where the Prophet ﷺ, Ali (RA), and some early companions were found praying in a valley by Abu Talib, who asked what they were doing — and the Prophet ﷺ explained the prayer. Abu Talib did not accept Islam himself but told his nephew to continue, and pledged his protection.

The Quran revealed during this early period emphasizes tawhid (the oneness of Allah), the reality of the afterlife, accountability for deeds, and the nobility of the poor and oppressed. Surahs such as al-Fatiha, al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq, al-Nas, al-Asr, and numerous others from the early Makkan revelation were memorized and practiced by the first community. Al-Tabari notes that by the time the open call began, there were approximately thirty to forty Muslims in Makkah.
